name: Decomposing Predictive Kubernetes Autoscaling for Large Language Model Serving Under Long Startup Delays
affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
problem: New serving replicas take 2-10 MINUTES to start because multi-gigabyte weights must load, which makes purely reactive autoscaling structurally late — no amount of reaction speed can beat the actuation delay.
mechanism: Decompose predictive autoscaling into four factors — token-aware demand tracking, startup-delay lookahead, a bounded uncertainty margin, and plant-state observation — and measure each factor's contribution in isolation on production-derived heavy-tailed workloads from ServeGen. Conclusion: a simple exponentially weighted moving average with delay-aware lookahead and an upper-confidence-bound margin captures most of the benefit.
speedup_reported: Per the arXiv abstract: reduces TTFT SLO violations from 53% (reactive, queries-per-second based) to 0.5% across five random seeds; lookahead alone is the single largest factor at a 14x reduction. Explicit negative result also reported: Kalman-filter variants do NOT consistently beat the EWMA. This is a usefulness result about scheduler DEPLOYMENT rather than request-level throughput — the baseline is reactive QPS-based scaling, which is the weak baseline it should be compared against.
notes: VENUE CAVEAT, stated plainly: the arXiv comment field says 'accepted by CloudCom 2026' and that is my ONLY evidence — I did not confirm it against a CloudCom proceedings page, so the venue is recorded as arxiv-preprint and CloudCom is not in the schema enum regardless. This is the scheduling-plane counterpart to the data-plane scheduling papers above and covers the layer most serving papers ignore: adding capacity. The negative result (Kalman filters lose to EWMA) is the most transferable finding.
